transcript:
Header:
Date: 2026-12-14
Start: 16:10 PST | Duration: 43 min
Attendees: Maya (Redwood AE), Ravi (Redwood SE), Ellen (CTO), Marco (Lead ML Eng), Sana (PM)

Topics: quick sandbox walkthrough, streaming behaviour, params (temp/top_p/stop), retries/backoff, KV cache, console metrics, security questions (SOC2/KMS/SSO), next steps and POC scope

[00:00] Maya: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, I'm Maya from Redwood, and with me is Ravi our solutions engineer. Uh, how's everybody doing?
[00:05] Ellen: Good, thanks. Quick note, we're coming from a hospital environment so PM and data privacy are the big concerns for us.
[00:12] Marco: Yes, hi all. We want to understand streaming latency and failure modes, and whether hosted is safe for PHI or we need private.
[00:19] Ravi: Totally, we'll cover both hosted behaviors and what changes if you move to Private or Dedicated. Today we'll demo the hosted sandbox first, show streaming, retries, and the Console's tracing.
[00:27] Sana: Great, and can we see how to tune temperature and top_p for the triage assistant we mentioned?
[00:34] Maya: Yep. Quick agenda: 1) Quick API live run, 2) Console traces and cost metrics, 3) Retry patterns and fallback to smaller quantized model, 4) Security/archives briefly, then Q&A.
[00:47] Ravi: I'm going to share my screen — ok you should see the sandbox project in the Redwood Console. I have a small curl and node example on the right.
[01:02] Ravi: (typing) So here's a streaming chat call to the /v1/chat/stream endpoint, we set streaming: true. You'll notice the SDK returns chunks as Server-Sent Events.
[01:16] Marco: Is the streaming chunk size configurable? Like can we control how often we flush tokens?
[01:22] Ravi: There's not a single "chunk size" parameter, it's a combination of model response speed and server flush policy. You can adjust the chunking by setting the generation param "stream_interval_ms" in the Console or use a smaller max_new_tokens to get earlier flushes. Also batching interacts — if you enable large batching you'll see more latency in first token.
[01:41] Ellen: So batching is for throughput, but we need first-byte latency under 200ms for certain flows. Can hosted meet that?
[01:49] Ravi: For many workloads yes, depending on model and sequence length. Our recommended pattern: prefer lower batching, enable prefix KV caching for repeated system prompts, and pin to a low-latency model variant. We also route by latency SLOs.
[02:04] Sana: What's KV caching? I think I heard K V cash in another call.
[02:08] Ravi: (laughs) Yeah transcripts sometimes show K V cash. KV cache is the key-value cache of past tokens for decoder models, we store and reuse cached attention keys for prompt prefixes so you don't recompute the same prefix every time. That saves time.
[02:22] Marco: If we use KV caching, does it keep any user PII? How's it encrypted?
[02:27] Ravi: Good point. On hosted, transient KV entries are encrypted at rest and in transit; persistent caches can be configured to be customer-specific. For PHI we usually recommend Private or Dedicated with customer KMS so you control keys and retention.
[02:40] Ellen: That aligns with our security posture. What certifications do you have?
[02:43] Maya: Redwood has SOC 2 Type II, and we're working through enterprise contracts. For Private deployments we support customer-managed KMS/HSM and VPC peering — we'll attach our security packet after.
[02:55] Marco: Please include audit log format in that packet.
[02:58] Maya: Will do.
[03:00] Ravi: Back to streaming: I'll run a live prompt. (keystrokes) Sending a conversation where system: "You are a triage assistant" and user: "Patient with chest pain, vitals..."
[03:14] [00:03:14] System: request sent
[03:16] [00:03:16] Ravi (transcribing): You might see the token stream come in as incremental SSEs, here's the first chunk.
[03:26] [00:03:26] (audio overlap) Marco: There's a slight stutter on our end — might be network.
[03:30] Ravi: Sorry if that's noisy. The first byte arrived around ~180ms in our test in us-west-2 for this short sequence.
[03:37] Ellen: How do you measure that in Console? Where's first-byte latency shown?
[03:41] Ravi: In Console > Metrics we show p50/p95 first-byte, server processing time, and token cost. You can also trace a single request and see the step times: receive, queue, model decode, and flush.
[03:55] Sana: Can we see a trace now?
[03:57] Ravi: Sure. (navigates) This trace shows a warm model hit with KV cache — notice model decode is much lower than cold start. Also you'll see a retry event here — the SDK retried once after a transient 503.
[04:12] Marco: How do retries work? If we get partial stream and then an error, can we resume?
[04:17] Ravi: Good question. With streaming, idempotency is trickier. Our SDK supports resumable streams for some failure modes by reissuing with the partial token offset and the model's KV state, but full resume requires that the model variant supports cross-request KV restoration. For many applications we implement client-side ordering: detect truncation, mark response incomplete, and either request regeneration or fall back to a non-streamed sync call.
[04:46] Ellen: So is the recommendation to do short lived retries or to fallback to a smaller model?
[04:51] Ravi: Both are patterns. We recommend exponential backoff with jitter for transient 5xxs. For capacity-driven failures, a useful fallback is a quantized variant with lower latency (and slightly lower quality). Console lets you configure automatic fallback policies per route.
[05:05] Sana: Can the fallback be to an on-prem version?
[05:09] Maya: In Private deployments you can define a local fallback. Hosted has fallbacks to our hosted quantized variants. For hybrid it's possible but requires network paths and routing profiles — we can scope that in POC.
[05:22] Marco: Any hard limits in hosted for streaming token rate? We process long conversations (~3k tokens).
[05:28] Ravi: There are model-specific sequence limits. Long context increases cost and memory. We support continuous KV caching to avoid re-sending entire history; you can evict older context or summarize with an embedding-based windowing strategy. For very long contexts we recommend Dedicated or on-prem for large memory GPUs.
[05:46] Ellen: Ok, let's talk about params. How do we tune temperature/top_p and stop sequences for consistent triage answers?
[05:53] Ravi: For deterministic extraction (e.g., triage code), we recommend low temperature (0–0.2) and narrower top_p (~0.6–0.8), and explicit stop tokens to avoid hallucination. For more creative suggestions, higher temperature. Also use system prompts to constrain behavior.
[06:10] Sana: Can we set those defaults per route in Console?
[06:14] Ravi: Yes, you can define route-level defaults for params, and override per request. Console also supports parameter presets and quick A/B toggles so you can test different param sets and compare quality and cost.
[06:26] Marco: How does cost vary with temperature?
[06:29] Ravi: Temperature doesn't change token counts — cost is per token computed. But higher temperature can produce longer outputs if not constrained, so indirectly affects cost. More important are max_tokens, top_p which can lead to longer generation.
[06:41] Ellen: We need predictable unit economics for budgeting. What visibility do we get?
[06:46] Maya: Console provides token-level cost breakdowns by route, model, and user token. We can also export CSVs for finance and set per-route quotas and alerts.
[06:55] Sana: Walkthrough of SDK example?
[06:58] Ravi: (shares code) Here's node: gen = client.chat.stream({ model: 'redwood-small-01', messages, stream: true, temperature: 0.1 }); gen.on('data', chunk => { /* assemble */ }); gen.on('end', ...)
[07:15] Marco: How are SSE disconnects handled? If connection drops, do we get partial text?
[07:20] Ravi: You'll get what was emitted. To avoid data loss, we recommend client ACKs or seq numbers in chunks, plus storing partial results server-side as you receive them. For critical flows you can then re-request the final sync generation to get a canonical response.
[07:33] Ellen: Is there an idempotency token we can use for sync calls?
[07:36] Ravi: Yes, for non-streamed calls we support idempotency keys. For streamed calls we advise application-level dedupe since replays may yield different tokens if not deterministic.
[07:49] Sana: Let's hit the Console Optimize section — suggestions, recommendations?
[07:52] Ravi: Optimize analyzes traffic patterns and suggests batching, quantization profiles, and which models to pin based on cost/latency tradeoffs. For example, it may suggest using redwood-quant-02 for low-cost fallback on non-critical paths.
[08:05] Marco: Can Optimize run evals on our in-house prompts?
[08:08] Ravi: Yes, you can upload prompt sets and golden answers; Optimize will run head-to-head comparisons and surface quality regressions. Very useful pre/post-quantization.
[08:18] Ellen: Security specifics — SSO and audit logs.
[08:21] Maya: We integrate with SAML/SSO providers, support RBAC with fine-grained roles, and provide audit logs you can forward to your SIEM. In Private you get additional network controls.
[08:33] Marco: Any additional compliance add-ons?
[08:35] Maya: We offer a compliance package that includes longer audit retention, monthly reviews, and contractual language around data handling — we'll include the PDF.
[08:44] Sana: Pricing? We need rough hosted numbers for planning.
[08:47] Maya: I won't go into full contract numbers on the call, but general hosted pricing is usage-based per token and embeddings. I'll send the hosted vs dedicated model with example math for your expected volume.
[08:58] Ravi: Back to failure modes: here's an example where the model returned partial stream then a 429 due to rate limits. We show the client-side retry with exponential backoff, and Console traces the retries.
[09:12] Marco: Can we set per-API key rate limits?
[09:15] Maya: Yes — rate limits and quotas can be set at token and request rates per key or per route. That helps protect downstream services.
[09:24] Ellen: Network egress concerns: if hosted, do you support regional hosting or data residency?
[09:29] Maya: Hosted API is available in multiple regions and we have controls for data residency; for strict in-country requirements we recommend Private. We'll map available regions in the follow-up.
[09:40] Sana: Any gotchas with streaming vs sync in mobile clients?
[09:43] Ravi: Mobile networks can be flaky. For mobile we often use short streaming chunks for responsiveness and then finalize with a sync confirmation for critical outputs. Also ensure tokenization is consistent across client and server to avoid partial token splits.
[10:00] Marco: Can you demo a retry scenario now?
[10:03] Ravi: Sure — I'll artificially throttle the route. (type) Triggering a 503, SDK retries twice with backoff. You can see in Console the request timeline and the second successful attempt.
[10:19] Maya: Note that repeated retries can increase cost — so set a sensible retry policy.
[10:23] Ellen: Understood.
[10:25] Sana: Any common misconfigurations customers make?
[10:28] Ravi: A few: 1) forgetting to set stop tokens leading to runaway outputs, 2) over-batching for low-latency paths, 3) not using KV caching for repeated prompts, and 4) expecting host-level KMS when using hosted without opting into customer-managed keys.
[10:46] Marco: For the POC, we want to simulate 1k concurrent users and a 95th latency of <400ms. Do you have reference architectures?
[10:54] Ravi: Yes, we'll put together an architecture doc showing autoscale settings, burst pools, pinning models for cold start reduction, and request shaping. For higher concurrency we recommend Dedicated reserved capacity.
[11:10] Ellen: Let's talk governance — who sees the logs and how long are they stored?
[11:14] Maya: Default is 30 days for hosted traces; we can extend retention as an add-on. You control access via RBAC and can export logs to your cloud storage for long-term retention. For PHI workflows we recommend Private + customer storage.
[11:28] Marco: Any latency penalty for encryption-at-rest with customer KMS?
[11:32] Ravi: Minimal; the main penalty is in key retrieval once per session. We cache encryption keys to avoid per-request HSM hits.
[11:41] Sana: I have a quick question on cost metrics per feature flag: can we see A/B differences in token cost?
[11:46] Ravi: Yes — Console has per-route breakdowns and you can tag requests with experiment IDs so Optimize surfaces A/B cost and quality deltas.
[11:56] Maya: Ok we're about 30 minutes in, we're going to wrap with final POC notes and next steps. Anything else urgent?
[12:02] Marco: One ask: include a small benchmark run that replicates our 3k token median session, and include p50/p95 numbers.
[12:08] Maya: Noted — action item.
[12:11] Sana: Also include the sample security packet and audit log schema.
[12:14] Maya: Yup. We'll send both.
[12:17] Ellen: Thanks, this was helpful.
[12:19] Maya: Great. Recap of next steps: Ravi shares sandbox credentials and SDK snippets; Maya sends pricing and security docs; Marco will send sample prompts; schedule POC kickoff.
[12:33] (crosstalk, goodbyes)

End of transcript.
